title: Can users publish video via the YouTube API through our UI, within quotas, verification and terms, or should we host it?
summary: YouTube Data API v3 upload quota cost, daily quota, restricted-scope verification, uploads from unverified apps, captions and transcripts, chapters, embed rules; Cloudflare Stream / Mux as the self-hosted alternative; a hybrid where YouTube hosts and we structure.

title: The site's existing YouTube labs use only the IFrame Player API - no Data API
summary: public/imagine/youtube/ (6 labs) and public/imagine/feeds/video/ (repo paths, read 2026-09-04) load https://www.youtube.com/iframe_api and youtube-nocookie.com embeds only, for playback control (Player wrapper, cues() timeline polled via getCurrentTime). Neither reads nor writes via googleapis.com/youtube/v3. No upload, no metadata read, no captions anywhere in the repo today.

title: videos.insert has its own quota bucket: 100 calls/day, 1 unit each, per Google's live reference doc
summary: Fetched developers.google.com/youtube/v3/docs/videos/insert directly (raw HTML, 2026-09-04): Quota impact: 100 calls per day. A call to this method has a quota cost of 1 unit in the Video Uploads quota bucket. Also: Maximum file size 256GB; MIME types video/* or application/octet-stream. This bucket is separate from the 10,000-unit general pool.

title: Unverified API projects created after 28 July 2020 can only upload videos as private
summary: Exact quote from the videos.insert reference page (fetched 2026-09-04): All videos uploaded via the videos.insert endpoint from unverified API projects created after 28 July 2020 will be restricted to private viewing mode. To lift this restriction, each API project must undergo an audit to verify compliance with the Terms of Service. This is the single biggest blocker to letting users publish public video through our UI as an MVP.

title: Many 2026 sources, and Google's own AI page summary, still say videos.insert costs 1600 units, not 100/day
summary: The determine_quota_cost page's own auto-generated Page Summary blurb (fetched 2026-09-04, same page as the table) says: methods like videos.insert have the highest cost of 1600 points - contradicting its own table 30 lines below, which says insert: 100 quota per day, 1 quota per call. Third-party 2026 posts (getphyllo.com, socialcrawl.dev) also state 1600 units flat with no mention of a dedicated bucket. The reference doc (videos/insert) agrees with the table, not the summary blurb - treated as authoritative here, but this is a live self-contradiction on Google's own docs.

title: Has anyone actually verified in production that a project can make 100 videos.insert calls a day in 2026?
summary: Every dated primary source we found agrees on the 100-calls/day, 1-unit-each bucket (2026-09-04), but this reverses years of tooling and blog posts built around the older ~6-uploads/day math from a 1600-unit cost, and we found no practitioner report confirming the new number empirically. Verify with a real test project before sizing the MVP around 100 uploads/day per project.

title: Default daily quota: 10,000 units for most endpoints, plus separate 100/day buckets for search.list and videos.insert
summary: Quoted directly from developers.google.com/youtube/v3/determine_quota_cost (last updated 2026-09-04 UTC): Projects that enable the YouTube Data API have a default quota allocation of 100 search.list calls, 100 videos.insert calls, and 10,000 units per day combined for all other endpoints. Daily quotas reset at midnight Pacific Time.

title: OAuth restricted-scope security assessment costs 15000 to 75000 USD/year, per third-party developer reports
summary: Google's own restricted-scope-verification page (fetched 2026-09-04) requires an annual third-party security assessment for restricted scopes stored/transmitted through a server but publishes no price. The commonly cited figure, from developer accounts, not Google: 15000-75000 USD or more, paid to a Google-approved assessor, redone every 12 months after the Letter of Assessment date (gmass.co blog, nylas.com blog). This tier is for restricted scopes (e.g. Gmail, Drive); we found no source stating youtube.upload is on that restricted list - see the linked question.

title: Is youtube.upload a sensitive scope (cheap, fast) or a restricted scope (CASA, 15k-75k/year)?
summary: Google classifies scopes as non-sensitive/sensitive/restricted dynamically inside Cloud Console when a project adds them - there is no static public list we could find that names youtube.upload's tier. Every practitioner report we read (postproxy.dev 2026 guide) describes only the lighter sensitive-scope path for YouTube upload: a use-case writeup, a demo video, ~3-5 business days per Google's sensitive-scope page (postproxy says plan 2-4 weeks including YouTube's own compliance audit). Nobody we found reports paying the CASA fee for youtube.upload specifically. Confirm in the actual Cloud Console before budgeting for a 15k+ assessment.

title: Sensitive-scope verification: a use-case writeup + demo video, about 3-5 business days
summary: Google's sensitive-scope-verification page (fetched 2026-09-04): the process needs a detailed justification per scope, a demo video showing the OAuth grant and the scope's use in the app, and states the sensitive scope verification process typically takes 3-5 business days to complete, with a 7-day window to publish before re-verification is needed. No fee is mentioned on this page.

title: The unverified-app warning screen caps an app at 100 new users total
summary: Google's Unverified apps support page (fetched 2026-09-04): once an app presents the unverified app screen (Google hasn't verified this app), it is capped at 100 new users in total. Apps in development/testing mode are exempt from verification. This matters if we let early users connect their own YouTube channel before our project passes verification.

title: captions.download costs 200 quota units and needs the video owner's OAuth
summary: developers.google.com/youtube/v3/docs/captions/download (fetched 2026-09-04): quota cost 200 units per call; requires the youtube.force-ssl or youtubepartner scope; the page states this method requires the user to have permission to edit the video. So captions/transcripts are only readable through the API for videos our own connected OAuth user owns - not arbitrary public videos.

title: The YouTube API Services ToS explicitly bans scraping, including scraped transcripts
summary: Quoted verbatim from developers.google.com/youtube/terms/developer-policies (fetched 2026-09-04), section on Scraping: You and your API Clients must not, and must not encourage, enable, or require others to, directly or indirectly, scrape YouTube Applications or Google Applications, or obtain scraped YouTube data or content. Public search engines may scrape data only in accordance with YouTube's robots.txt file or with YouTube's prior written permission. Pulling transcripts from unofficial youtube-transcript style libraries for videos we do not own is a ToS violation, not a legal gray area for us specifically.

title: The API Services ToS 30-day rule: non-authorized stats never exceed 30 days; authorized data needs re-verified consent every 30 days
summary: Quoted from developers.google.com/youtube/terms/developer-policies (fetched 2026-09-04): an API Client must not store statistics retrieved as Non-Authorized Data (view counts, subscriber counts, etc pulled without that user's own consent) for more than 30 days. Authorized Data (data the connected user consented to) may be kept longer than 30 days only if the Client verifies every 30 days that authorization has not been revoked and the source video/channel still exists - never longer than 30 calendar days without that re-check.

title: COPPA / Made for Kids: child-directed API clients cannot take write actions on YouTube at all
summary: Per Google's developer-policies page (search result quoting the ToS, 2026): an API Client targeting children under COPPA must let users flag content Made for Kids before upload, or send them to youtube.com to do it. Child-Directed API Clients and their users must not take any YouTube API Services write-based actions (uploads, edits) - uploads from known Child-Directed API Clients are not implemented on YouTube at all. This closes off an API-driven kids-content upload flow entirely, by policy, not just quota.

title: IFrame embed rules: 200x200px minimum, no overlays, no player modifications, autoplay only if half-visible
summary: Quoted from developers.google.com/youtube/terms/required-minimum-functionality (fetched 2026-09-04): Embedded players must have a viewport that is at least 200px by 200px (480x270 recommended for 16:9). You must not display overlays, frames, or other visual elements in front of any part of a YouTube embedded player, including player controls. Must not make changes to the player not described in the API docs. Autoplay only once the player is more than half visible; only one autoplaying player per page.

title: Resumable upload chunks must be multiples of 256KB; a partial success returns HTTP 308
summary: Quoted from developers.google.com/youtube/v3/guides/using_resumable_upload_protocol (fetched 2026-09-04): The chunk size must be a multiple of 256 KB (last chunk exempt); larger chunks are more efficient; each chunk PUT sets Content-Range (e.g. bytes 0-524287/2000000); a non-final successful chunk gets a 308 Resume Incomplete response so the client can resume after a drop.

title: Google does not document CORS support for browser-direct resumable uploads to YouTube
summary: Neither the client-side-web-apps OAuth guide nor the resumable-upload guide (both fetched 2026-09-04) mention CORS, cross-origin headers, or browser-direct upload at all - both assume a server or the JS client library. Practitioner reports (a 2013 blog, scattered GitHub issues) say XHR/fetch uploads to googleapis.com/upload/youtube/v3/videos do work with an access token, but others report CORS errors. Treat browser-direct upload as unsupported/unverified, not a documented capability.

title: Cloudflare Workers request body limit: 100MB Free/Pro, 200MB Business, up to 5GB Enterprise self-serve
summary: Quoted from developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/limits (fetched 2026-09-04): request body size depends on the account plan not the Workers plan - Free 100MB, Pro 100MB, Business 200MB, Enterprise up to 5GB self-serve (adjustable from the zone Network page), more by contacting sales. Requests over the limit get a 413. A typical uploaded video easily exceeds 100-200MB, so proxying full video bodies through our own Worker is a real ceiling on Free/Pro/Business plans.

title: Cloudflare Stream:  per 1000 min stored (prepaid),  per 1000 min delivered, encoding free, 30GB max file
summary: Quoted from developers.cloudflare.com/stream/pricing (dateModified 2026-09-01, fetched 2026-09-04): Storage is a prepaid pricing dimension purchased in increments of  per 1,000 minutes stored, regardless of file size. Delivery is a post-paid, usage-based pricing dimension billed at  per 1,000 minutes delivered. Ingress and encoding are always free; bandwidth is included in delivery with no separate egress fee. Max file size 30GB.

title: Cloudflare Stream cost at 1k/10k hours stored and delivered: 00/0 and 000/000
summary: Derived from Stream's own unit prices (see the /1000min-stored, /1000min-delivered entry): 1,000 hours = 60,000 minutes. Stored: 60,000/1000 x  = 00 one-time capacity purchase. Delivered: 60,000/1000 x  = 0 for 1,000 hours of total viewing. At 10,000 hours: storage ,000, delivery ,000 for 10,000 viewer-hours. Delivery scales with total watch time across all viewers, not per-video.

title: Mux: storage from /usr/bin/bash.0024/min/month (720p, basic/plus), first 100,000 delivered min/month free, then /usr/bin/bash.0008/min
summary: Quoted from mux.com/docs/pricing.txt (fetched 2026-09-04): basic-quality input (encoding) is free; basic/plus storage up to 720p is /usr/bin/bash.002400 per minute per month (first 50,000-minute tier, volume discounts beyond); delivery gives the first 100,000 minutes delivered each month free regardless of quality, then /usr/bin/bash.000800/min (first 500,000-minute tier) for up to 720p, more for higher resolutions.

title: Mux cost at 1k/10k hours stored and delivered (720p, basic/plus): roughly 44/mo and /usr/bin/bash first tier, then scaling
summary: Derived from Mux's own unit prices: 1,000 hours stored/month = 60,000 min x /usr/bin/bash.0024 = 44/month recurring (vs Cloudflare Stream's 00 one-time). 1,000 hours delivered/month = 60,000 min, entirely inside the 100,000-free-minute allowance = /usr/bin/bash. 10,000 hours stored = 600,000 min x ~/usr/bin/bash.00224-0.0024 blended = roughly ,400-1,440/month; 10,000 hours delivered = 600,000 min, minus 100,000 free = 500,000 min x /usr/bin/bash.0008 = 00.

title: Bunny Stream: storage /usr/bin/bash.01/GB/month, CDN delivery /usr/bin/bash.005-0.01/GB depending on region/tier
summary: Quoted from docs.bunny.net/stream/pricing (fetched 2026-09-04): default region (e.g. Frankfurt) storage is /usr/bin/bash.01/GB; Standard network delivery is /usr/bin/bash.010/GB (Europe and North America, higher elsewhere); the Volume network tier starts at /usr/bin/bash.005/GB for 0-500TB/month, down to /usr/bin/bash.002/GB above 1000TB. Unlike Stream/Mux this is billed per GB transferred, not per minute - cost depends on bitrate, so it is cheaper for lower-bitrate or aggressively compressed video and pricier at high bitrate/4K.

title: R2 storage is /usr/bin/bash.015/GB-month with free egress, but has no encoding, ABR, or player built in
summary: Quoted from developers.cloudflare.com/r2/pricing (last updated 2026-08-07, fetched 2026-09-04): Standard storage /usr/bin/bash.015/GB-month, Class A ops .50/million, Class B ops /usr/bin/bash.36/million, egress always free. Free tier: 10GB-month storage, 1M Class A, 10M Class B ops/month. R2 is object storage only - it does no transcoding, adaptive bitrate packaging, thumbnailing, or analytics; those would have to be built or bolted on separately (ffmpeg in a Worker/container, a hand-rolled HLS packager, a player).

title: R2 + hand-built HLS is not worth it before a platform truly needs multi-bitrate video at scale
summary: R2's price is the best of the four options per GB, but Stream/Mux/Bunny each already include transcoding, packaging, a player, and (Stream/Mux) analytics for close to the same money once you count viewer minutes, not just storage. Building our own encoder pipeline and HLS packager on R2 is a multi-week project that duplicates a commodity. Reasonable only for serving pre-encoded single-rendition MP4 progressive files (e.g. short platform-native clips capped at one resolution) where adaptive bitrate does not matter yet.

title: DMCA safe harbor needs a registered designated agent, notice-and-takedown, and a repeat-infringer policy
summary: Standard US platform-law requirements (Copyright Alliance / Harris Sliwoski / Congress.gov summaries, 2026): register a designated DMCA agent (name, address, phone, email) with the US Copyright Office's online system and publish it on the site; respond to takedown notices and honor counter-notices; adopt and reasonably enforce a policy that terminates repeat infringers' accounts; do not interfere with standard technical measures used to detect infringement. Losing the safe harbor exposes the platform to direct copyright liability for user uploads.

title: Chapters and thumbnails need no special API access - description text and videos.list snippet cover both
summary: YouTube auto-generates chapters from timestamp lines in the video description (a creator convention, not a distinct write field); reading a video's description via videos.list (1 unit, snippet part) is enough to parse the same timestamps ourselves for our own topic structure. Thumbnail URLs (default/medium/high) are also included in videos.list snippet.thumbnails at no extra quota cost - no separate thumbnails endpoint call needed for read-only display.

title: Correction: entries 20-25 above lost every dollar figure to a shell quoting bug
summary: Double-quoted bash arguments let $ expand as shell variables, stripping every dollar amount from the Cloudflare Stream, Mux, Bunny Stream and R2 pricing entries above (titles and summaries both). This log is append-only so those lines stay, but treat their numbers as unreadable - the correct figures are re-entered in the findings immediately following this one, written with single-quoted arguments instead.

summary: Quoted from developers.cloudflare.com/r2/pricing (last updated 2026-08-07, fetched 2026-09-04): Standard storage $0.015/GB-month, Class A ops $4.50/million, Class B ops $0.36/million, egress always free. Free tier: 10GB-month storage, 1M Class A, 10M Class B ops/month. R2 is object storage only - no transcoding, adaptive bitrate packaging, thumbnailing, or analytics; those would have to be built separately (ffmpeg in a Worker/container, a hand-rolled HLS packager, a player).

title: youtube-nocookie.com defers all cookies until play - the GDPR-safe embed mode, already in use on this site
summary: Loading a YouTube embed from youtube-nocookie.com instead of youtube.com is the documented privacy-enhanced mode: no personalization cookies are set until the viewer presses play. Both existing labs (public/imagine/youtube and public/imagine/feeds/video) already build the poster synchronously and only swap in a youtube-nocookie.com iframe on click, so this pattern is proven and ready to reuse for any embedded video the platform ships.

title: MVP recommendation: embed and structure YouTube video, do not build upload-through-our-UI yet
summary: The challenge asked whether upload-through-our-interface belongs in the MVP. Against it: unverified projects upload private-only until a compliance audit passes (finding above), OAuth verification for youtube.upload takes days-to-weeks even in the best case, CORS for a true browser-direct upload is undocumented, and our own Worker cannot proxy full video bodies past 100-200MB on Free/Pro/Business plans. For it: 100 calls/day at 1 unit each is not quota-constrained if the number holds up. Net: embedding and metadata-driven structuring are cheap and proven today; upload is a real feature but not a fast one, and should wait for a passed compliance audit, not block the MVP.

title: YouTube hosting is not free for us in any sense that matters once uploads and API reads enter the picture
summary: Embedding costs nothing (no quota, no fee) and is what the site already does. But the moment we add uploads or metadata reads through the Data API we inherit: quota management, an annual-or-one-time verification process with real calendar time and possibly real dollars, a 30-day data retention rule to engineer around, scraping and COPPA restrictions, and total dependence on a platform we do not control for content that may be central to the product. Free-as-in-embed is real; free-as-in-integrated-upload-platform is not.

title: Transcripts are not freely obtainable for arbitrary videos - only for ones we have the owning OAuth for, or via a manual creator paste
summary: The challenge asked whether transcripts are obtainable. captions.download needs the video owner permission (finding above, 200 units); scraping third-party transcripts is a explicit ToS violation (finding above, quoted). So for the hybrid model, automatic transcript import only works for creators who connect their own YouTube OAuth to our platform. Everyone else either types/pastes a transcript manually or gets none - transcripts are not a free universal feature of embedding someone elses public video.

title: Automatic structuring is a metadata parse, not a Data API problem - title/description/chapters are already free reads
summary: Title, description (with its chapter timestamps) and thumbnails all come from one 1-unit videos.list call for videos we have a URL/ID for at all - no OAuth needed for public metadata. Turning that into topic sections is a text-parsing and AI-summarization problem, not a quota or access problem. What model does the summarizing is out of scope here per the brief - left to the ai research topic.

title: Does public metadata (title/description/thumbnails) really need zero OAuth, or does an API key still gate videos.list?
summary: We read this as true from the quota table and reference docs (videos.list costs 1 unit, no owner-scope requirement listed) but did not run a live unauthenticated videos.list call against a real API key to confirm no OAuth step is required for public video metadata - only that the docs do not list one. Worth a five-minute smoke test with a real API key before relying on it.
